# Step 6: Routes: how goods got around the blockade, and how far supply chains came back

*Generated by `src/routes.py` (charts and text by `src/step6_report.py`). Re-running the script refreshes every number.*

Step 5 measured how far imports fell below normal. This step looks at **how** goods reach Bahrain, and asks four questions:

1. Which routes were cut, and for how long?
2. Did goods that could use routes that stayed open hold up better?
3. How much must have come by road, a route with no published figures?
4. How far had each supply chain come back, and is it still adapting?

## The short answer

| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| Which routes were cut? | **Container ships:** containers unloaded at the port fell to about a third of normal from March to July (33%, 32% and 30% in March, Apr-May and Jun-Jul). **Car carriers stopped completely** from April (still none in September). **Planes:** air cargo was almost zero in March, when the airspace was closed, and back to 70% of normal by Jun-Jul. |
| Did goods that could use open routes hold up better? | **Yes.** Goods from **GCC countries**, which can come by road, were +8% against the forecast from Mar-Jul (inside the normal range), and +19% in Jun-Jul. Goods from **beyond the Middle East** were -40%. Among those, while Hormuz was shut but the airspace open (April-May), **light goods held up far better than heavy goods**: -13% against -54% (leaving out aircraft engines, which are bought irregularly). |
| How much must have come by road? | **At least half.** Container ships and planes could have carried at most 46% of core goods by weight from Mar-Jul. So **at least 54% (about 660 thousand tonnes) came by road over the King Fahd Causeway, or by general cargo ship.** The data can't fully separate those two. |
| How far had supply chains come back? | **About two-thirds of the way** by Jun-Jul: from 46% of normal in March to 82%. Europe, South Asia and the rest of the Middle East were back inside their normal range (goods from GCC countries were above normal), as were 9 of 18 product sections; **vehicles (54%), East Asia (61%) and the Americas (61%) were still far below**. |
| Is it still adapting? | **The port figures say yes.** They run two months ahead of the import data: even after Hormuz closed again on 11 July, containers unloaded rose from 30% of normal in Jun-Jul to 47% in Aug-Sep. Car carriers still hadn't returned. |

## Words used in this report

| Word | What it means here |
|---|---|
| **Core goods** | All imports except bulk materials (iron ore, alumina, coke and construction minerals) and precious metals (gold, silver and jewellery). These are the everyday supply chains, about three-quarters of import value. |
| **National total** (also *nationally* or *All of Bahrain*) | All core goods imports into Bahrain in a month, added together: every product from every origin, in one number. It doesn't include bulk materials or precious metals, or oil (the portal's import data covers non-oil imports only). |
| **Origin region** | Where goods came from, grouped into 9 regions by how they normally reach Bahrain. **GCC** means Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Kuwait, Qatar and Oman, including the Jebel Ali and Oman free zones. |
| **Section** | One of the 21 top-level groups of the customs (HS) code, such as "Machinery and electrical" or "Vehicles and transport". Each section is made up of HS2 chapters. |
| **Series** | One line of monthly numbers: one HS2 chapter from one origin region, for example "chapter 84 (machinery) from Europe". |
| **Route** | How goods physically reach Bahrain: by container ship, car carrier or general cargo ship (all at Khalifa Bin Salman Port), by plane (Bahrain International Airport), or by truck over the King Fahd Causeway. |
| **King Fahd Causeway** | The 25 km road bridge between Saudi Arabia and Bahrain, Bahrain's only road link to the mainland. No monthly freight figures for it are published. |
| **TEU** | One twenty-foot shipping container. A standard forty-foot container counts as 2 TEU. |
| **Car carrier** (RoRo) | A "roll-on, roll-off" ship that vehicles are driven on and off. The port counts the vehicles unloaded. |
| **General cargo** | Goods that travel neither in containers nor loose in bulk, loaded piece by piece: steel, timber, machinery, bagged food, livestock. Counted in freight tonnes. |
| **Freight tonne** | A shipping unit: one tonne, or one cubic metre if the goods are bulky, whichever is larger. So freight tonnes are never less than the weight in tonnes. |
| **Normal** | Two meanings, one for each kind of data. For **imports**, normal means step 5's forecast: what was expected without the war. For **port and airport figures**, which have no forecast, normal means the same months of 2025. |
| **% of normal** | Actual as a percentage of normal: 100% is normal, 50% is half. (Step 5's gap of -54% is 46% of normal.) |
| **Forecast** | What the model expected imports to be **without the war**. It was made at the end of December 2025, so it never saw any 2026 data. |
| **Gap** | Actual imports minus the forecast: in BD, or as % of the forecast. Negative means below normal. |
| **Normal range** | How far from the forecast a total can be in a normal year (9 times out of 10), measured in step 4's tests. Longer periods have narrower ranges. |
| **Real shortfall** | A gap bigger than the normal range: too big to be ordinary ups and downs. |
| **Since the war** | March 2026 to the latest month the portal has published, added together. |
| **Beyond the Middle East** | Goods from Asia, Europe, the Americas, Africa and Oceania (plus a small "not specified" group). Before the war these came mostly by sea through the Strait of Hormuz, or by plane. |
| **Light, middle and heavy goods** | Series grouped by their value per kilogram in 2024-2025. **Light**: BD 5 per kg or more (about $13), worth flying: machinery and parts, medicines, instruments, watches, clothes. **Heavy**: under BD 1 per kg: steel, plastics, meat, fruit, rice, building materials. **Middle**: in between. Vehicles are kept apart because they travel on their own kind of ship. |
| **Elimination** | Working out how much came by a route with no figures (the road) by taking away the most the other routes could have carried. |
| **Came back ...% of the way** | How much of the drop had been made up by the latest period. From 46% of normal at the worst to 82% is (82 - 46) / (100 - 46) = two-thirds of the way. Over 100% means it ended above normal. |
| **Adapting** | Finding other ways to get goods in while the usual route is shut. Used instead of "recovery" because the Strait of Hormuz closed again on 11 July and was still closed in October. |
| **BD m, kt** | Million Bahraini dinars (value) and thousand tonnes (weight). |

---

## Before you start: how this step works

### Step 1: The five routes into Bahrain

Bahrain is an island. Goods arrive in one of five ways:

| Route | Where | What it carries | Monthly figures? |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Container ships** | Khalifa Bin Salman Port | Most manufactured goods from Asia, Europe and the Americas | Yes: containers unloaded (TEU), ship visits |
| **Car carriers (RoRo)** | Khalifa Bin Salman Port | New cars and other vehicles | Yes: vehicles unloaded |
| **General cargo ships** | Khalifa Bin Salman Port | Steel, timber, machinery, bagged food, livestock | Yes: freight tonnes handled, ship visits |
| **Planes** | Bahrain International Airport | Light, valuable or urgent goods | Yes: tonnes unloaded |
| **Trucks over the King Fahd Causeway** | From Saudi Arabia | Goods from GCC countries, and goods landed at their ports | **No** |

Everything that reaches Bahrain by sea from outside the Gulf passes through the **Strait of Hormuz**. The road comes
from Saudi Arabia, so it carries goods from GCC countries, and goods from further away that were landed at Saudi, UAE or
Omani ports and driven the rest of the way. **The road is the one route with no monthly figures**, so it has to be
worked out from the others (step 4 below).

### Step 2: Two kinds of "normal"

* **Imports** are compared with step 5's forecast of what would have arrived without the war, with the same normal ranges
  (a gap only counts as a real change when it is bigger than the model's normal misses).
* **Port and airport figures** have no forecast, so each 2026 month is compared with **the same month of 2025**. The
  changes are so large (often more than half) that the choice of comparison doesn't change the picture.

### Step 3: The periods

| Period | What was happening | Import data? |
|---|---|---|
| **Jan-Feb** | Before the war (it began on 28 February) | yes |
| **March** | The shock: Strait of Hormuz and Bahrain's airspace closed, Mina Salman Port struck | yes |
| **Apr-May** | Airspace reopened on 8 April, but Hormuz stayed closed and a US naval blockade began | yes |
| **Jun-Jul** | A brief, partial reopening of Hormuz from 18 June, then closed again on 11 July | yes |
| **Aug-Sep** | Hormuz closed again from 11 July (still closed in October) | not yet (port and airport figures only) |

The port and airport publish their figures about two months before the import data, so they show what happened in
Aug-Sep too.

### Step 4: Elimination, in plain words

Imagine 100 tonnes of goods arrived in a month, and the port says it unloaded a third as many containers as usual.

1. **The most the containers could have carried.** Pretend that last year *everything* came in containers. That's
   more than is true, so it gives the most containers could carry now: a third of last year's goods.
2. **Add everything that came by plane** (as if every tonne of air cargo were core goods, again more than is true).
3. **Whatever is left must have come another way:** by truck over the causeway, or by general cargo ship.

Because each step is deliberately generous to containers and planes, the answer is a **minimum** for the road and
general cargo ships together. It needs one assumption: that a container held no more than usual.

---

## 1. Which routes were cut?

![Routes](figures/step6_1_routes.png)

**What we did:** compared each port and airport figure for 2026 with the same months of 2025, and core goods imports by
weight with the same months of 2025.

**What we found (% of the same months in 2025):**

| Indicator | Jan-Feb | March | Apr-May | Jun-Jul | Aug-Sep |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Containers unloaded | 112% | 33% | 32% | 30% | 47% |
| Container ship visits | 82% | 33% | 53% | 61% | 83% |
| Vehicles unloaded from car carriers | 100% | 16% | 0% | 0% | 0% |
| General cargo handled | 70% | - | 292% | 281% | 548% |
| General cargo ship visits | 78% | 59% | 73% | 56% | 64% |
| Air cargo and mail unloaded | 103% | 1% | 31% | 70% | 69% |
| Core goods imported, by weight | 120% | 65% | 65% | 79% | - |

*A dash means no figure yet. General cargo jumps around from month to month (in 2025, from 12,372 to
105,028 freight tonnes), so against the 2025 average month, Aug-Sep 2026 was 3.5 times normal.*

1. **Containers fell by about two-thirds and stayed there.** From March to July the port unloaded about a third of the
   usual containers in every period. Fewer container ships called, and those that did unloaded less.
2. **Car carriers stopped.** Vehicles unloaded from car carriers fell to 16% of normal in March and to **zero from April**, still zero in September.
3. **Planes came back slowly.** Air cargo was 1% of normal in March (the airspace was closed until 8 April),
   31% in April-May and 70% in Jun-Jul. It never rose above normal.
4. **General cargo went the other way.** Fewer general cargo ships called, but in April-May they handled about 3 times
   the usual tonnage, and more after that.
5. **Core goods by weight fell much less than any of these:** 65% of normal in
   March, 79% in Jun-Jul.

**A data problem fixed along the way.** In the general cargo file, several 2026 months were typed with a decimal point
where a thousands separator belongs (56.186 instead of 56,186). Step 2 now repairs them and marks each one; they are the
open circles in the chart. March 2026 was recorded as 0 although 17 general cargo ships called, so it is treated as
missing.

**Why it matters:** goods kept arriving at 71% of their 2025 weight from Mar-Jul, while containers ran at a third. The difference had to come in some other way. Sections 2 and 3 work out how.

---

## 2. Did goods that could use open routes hold up better?

![Route groups](figures/step6_2_route_groups.png)

**What we did:** repeated step 5's comparison (actual imports against the forecast without the war, with the normal
ranges from step 4's tests) for groups of goods that depend on different routes.

### 2a. By where the goods came from

| Goods from | Share of normal imports | March | Apr-May | Jun-Jul | Mar-Jul | Normal range (Mar-Jul) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| GCC countries | 15% | -15% | +8% | +19% | +8% | +/-10% |
| the rest of the Middle East | 3% | -33% | -19% | -6% | -16% | +/-9% |
| beyond the Middle East | 82% | -62% | -44% | -25% | -40% | +/-5% |

1. **Goods from GCC countries held up**: +8% from Mar-Jul, inside the normal range.
   In Jun-Jul they were +19%, **above** normal (outside the range).
2. **Goods from the rest of the Middle East fell, but less**: -16%.
3. **Goods from beyond the Middle East fell furthest**: -40%, and -62% in March. They account for more than all of the money lost: BD 636m, against BD 624m nationally, because goods from GCC countries arrived BD 22m above normal.

### 2b. Goods from beyond the Middle East: light against heavy

Light goods are worth flying; heavy ones must go by sea or road. If planes helped, light goods should have held up better
once the airspace reopened on 8 April, while Hormuz was still shut.

| Goods from beyond the Middle East | Share of value | Share of weight | March | Apr-May | Jun-Jul | Mar-Jul |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Light goods | 31% | 3% | -74% | -25% | -17% | -31% |
| Middle | 34% | 20% | -46% | -43% | -27% | -37% |
| Heavy goods | 19% | 73% | -61% | -54% | -19% | -41% |
| Vehicles and transport | 16% | 4% | -68% | -75% | -46% | -62% |

One correction matters here. **Aircraft engines** are light and valuable, and one airline's purchases can move the light
group a lot: they almost stopped in March and came back irregularly (step 5 showed the same effect nationally). Holding
them at their normal level:

| Light goods from beyond the Middle East | March | Apr-May | Jun-Jul | Mar-Jul |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| As measured | -74% | -25% | -17% | -31% |
| With aircraft engines at their normal level | -42% | -13% | -16% | -20% |

1. **In March everything fell**, light goods included: the airspace was closed as well as the sea route.
2. **In April-May light goods held up far better:** -13% (without aircraft engines) against
   **-54% for heavy goods.** That is the period when planes could fly but ships couldn't pass Hormuz.
3. **In June-July heavy goods bounced back** to -19%. This was when Hormuz partly reopened
   (18 June to 11 July), and when general cargo, the usual way to ship heavy goods such as steel, timber and bagged rice,
   was about 3 times its usual tonnage.
4. **Vehicles stayed deepest**: -62% from Mar-Jul. Section 3 shows why.

Air cargo into Bahrain itself was only 31% of normal in April-May, so planes into Bahrain can't
be the whole story for light goods. Some probably flew into nearby Saudi airports and came over the causeway, or came in
the containers that still arrived.

**Why it matters:** the supply chains that held up were the ones with **another way in**: the road for goods from GCC
countries, planes (into Bahrain or nearby) for light goods. Heavy goods from far away had no other way in until ships could pass again.

---

## 3. How much must have come by road?

![Elimination](figures/step6_3_elimination.png)

**What we did:** the elimination from before-you-start, step 4, for each period, using core goods by weight.

**What we found:**

|  | March | Apr-May | Jun-Jul | Mar-Jul |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Core goods arriving, by weight (kt) | 199 | 443 | 592 | 1,234 |
| ... as % of the same months of 2025 | 65% | 65% | 79% | 71% |
| Containers unloaded, % of the same months of 2025 | 33% | 32% | 30% | 31% |
| Air cargo unloaded, % of the same months of 2025 | 1% | 31% | 70% | 39% |
| **Most that containers and planes could have carried** | **51%** | **52%** | **41%** | **46%** |
| **Least that came by road or general cargo ship** | **49% (98 kt)** | **48% (213 kt)** | **59% (351 kt)** | **54% (660 kt)** |
| Goods from GCC countries, share of the weight (2025 -> 2026) | 34% -> 52% | 35% -> 53% | 30% -> 41% | 32% -> 47% |

1. **At least 54% of what arrived from Mar-Jul came by road or general cargo ship**:
   about 660 thousand tonnes. In every period it was at least
   48%.
2. **This is a minimum.** It assumes that last year everything came in containers, which isn't true: goods from GCC
   countries alone were about 32% of the weight in 2025, and most of those normally come by
   road. The real share was higher.

**Road or general cargo ship?** The data can't fully split the two. In June-July, for example, at least 351 kt came by road or general cargo ship, and the port handled 283 thousand freight tonnes of general cargo. If every one of those were core goods imports, general cargo ships could have carried most of it; if few were, the causeway carried almost all of it. Two clues point to the road
carrying a large part:

* **Goods from GCC countries kept arriving at their usual weight** (103% of the same
  months of 2025), so their share of everything that arrived rose from 32% to
  47%. Most of these goods come from Saudi Arabia, over the causeway.
* **Cars kept arriving without car carriers.** From April no car carrier unloaded at the port, yet cars made in East
  Asia and Europe kept being imported from May, at 40-61% of their 2025 average month:

| Month (2026) | Vehicles unloaded from car carriers | ... % of the 2025 average month | Cars from East Asia and Europe (BD m) | ... % of the 2025 average month  |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| January | 3,869 | 104% | 27.7 | 89% |
| February | 4,641 | 125% | 37.7 | 121% |
| March | 609 | 16% | 10.3 | 33% |
| April | 0 | 0% | 1.5 | 5% |
| May | 0 | 0% | 12.3 | 40% |
| June | 0 | 0% | 19.1 | 61% |
| July | 0 | 0% | 14.5 | 46% |

  They must have come another way: most likely landed at another country's port and driven or trucked over the
  causeway, or packed in containers.

**Why it matters:** the King Fahd Causeway, and possibly short trips by general cargo ships within the Gulf, kept a large
share of Bahrain's supply chains running while the sea route was shut. Putting a number on the road alone needs
assumptions (how much a container holds, and how much of the general cargo was imports). That is the "what if" range
planned for after step 7.

## 4. How far had each supply chain come back?

![Adapting](figures/step6_4_adapting.png)

**What we did:** for every origin region and product section, took step 5's gaps as **% of normal** in each war period,
found the worst one, and measured how much of the drop had been made up by Jun-Jul.

**What we found:**

| Origin | March | Apr-May | Jun-Jul | Came back | Inside the normal range in Jun-Jul? |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **All of Bahrain** | 46% | 64% | 82% | 66% of the way | no |
| Africa | 64% | 81% | 55% | no: fell further | no |
| East and South-East Asia | 51% | 43% | 61% | 31% of the way | no |
| Americas | 31% | 52% | 61% | 44% of the way | no |
| Europe | 25% | 71% | 87% | 83% of the way | yes |
| Other Middle East | 67% | 81% | 94% | 83% of the way | yes |
| South Asia | 43% | 54% | 95% | 92% of the way | yes |
| GCC | 85% | 108% | 119% | above normal | no |
| Oceania | 16% | 39% | 124% | above normal | yes |

| Section | March | Apr-May | Jun-Jul | Came back | Inside the normal range in Jun-Jul? |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Vehicles and transport | 32% | 25% | 54% | 38% of the way | no |
| Wood and cork | 50% | 55% | 64% | 27% of the way | no |
| Textiles and clothing | 38% | 63% | 66% | 45% of the way | no |
| Footwear and headgear | 36% | 51% | 67% | 49% of the way | no |
| Hides, leather and travel goods | 32% | 67% | 69% | 54% of the way | yes |
| Miscellaneous manufactures | 56% | 70% | 74% | 42% of the way | no |
| Machinery and electrical | 30% | 56% | 75% | 65% of the way | no |
| Instruments and clocks | 31% | 86% | 82% | 74% of the way | no |
| Food, drinks and tobacco | 47% | 63% | 84% | 69% of the way | no |
| Paper | 64% | 73% | 88% | 66% of the way | yes |
| Stone, ceramics and glass | 59% | 70% | 93% | 82% of the way | yes |
| Base metals | 81% | 80% | 94% | 69% of the way | yes |
| Chemicals | 65% | 108% | 95% | 84% of the way | yes |
| Plastics and rubber | 61% | 67% | 95% | 87% of the way | yes |
| Minerals and fuels | 56% | 58% | 96% | 92% of the way | yes |
| Animal products | 61% | 80% | 97% | 93% of the way | yes |
| Fats and oils | 62% | 87% | 112% | above normal | yes |
| Vegetable products | 60% | 75% | 115% | above normal | no |

*Sections under 0.5% of the national forecast, and national special codes, are left out.*

1. **Nationally, imports came back about two-thirds of the way**: from
   46% of normal in March to 82% in Jun-Jul.
2. **Back inside the normal range by Jun-Jul:** Europe, South Asia, the rest of the Middle East and Oceania
   among origins, and 9 of 18 sections, including chemicals, base metals, animal products and plastics and rubber. **Above normal:** goods from GCC countries (119%) and vegetable products (115%).
3. **Still far below normal:** vehicles and transport (54%), wood and cork (64%), textiles and clothing (66%), footwear and headgear (67%) and miscellaneous manufactures (74%)
   among sections; Africa (55%), East and South-East Asia (61%) and the Americas (61%) among origins.

**A word of caution.** Part of the bounce in Jun-Jul came when Hormuz **partly reopened** (18 June to 11 July), so it
isn't all adapting: some ships that had been waiting got through. The clearest signs of adapting are the things that
improved **while Hormuz was shut**: light goods in April-May, goods from GCC countries above normal, and cars arriving
without car carriers.

---

## 5. What happened after July?

The import data stop at July, but the port and airport figures reach September.
Hormuz closed again on 11 July, so Aug-Sep is the first test of how well supply chains adapt to a closed strait without any help from a reopening.

| Indicator | Jun-Jul | Aug-Sep |
|---|---|---|
| Containers unloaded | 30% | 47% |
| Container ship visits | 61% | 83% |
| Vehicles unloaded from car carriers | 0% | 0% |
| General cargo handled | 281% | 548% |
| General cargo ship visits | 56% | 64% |
| Air cargo and mail unloaded | 70% | 69% |

1. **Containers kept climbing**: from 30% of normal in Jun-Jul to 47% in Aug-Sep, with Hormuz closed. More container ships called (83%). With the strait closed, they most likely came on ships from other ports inside the Gulf, carrying containers that had crossed land from ports outside it.
2. **Air cargo held at about 69% of normal.**
3. **Car carriers still hadn't returned**, and general cargo stayed high.

**Why it matters:** step 5's shortfall was shrinking while the strait was partly open. The port figures suggest the
supply chains kept adapting after it closed again. The import data for August, when published, will show whether the
goods themselves followed.

---

## What this step can't tell us

1. **The road has no figures.** Everything about the causeway is worked out from the other routes, so it is a minimum,
   not a measurement.
2. **The general cargo figures are the least reliable.** Several months had to be repaired, the file doesn't say whether
   it counts only goods unloaded or loaded too, and freight tonnes can be larger than the weight.
3. **Months don't line up exactly.** A ship's arrival and the customs record of its goods can fall in different months.
   Periods of two months or more soften this.
4. **Light, middle and heavy are rough groups.** They are decided for each series (one HS2 chapter from one region), so
   a few heavy items sit in light series and the other way round.

## What this means for step 7

Step 7 writes up the project. The main findings from this step:

1. **Containers and car carriers were cut; the road and general cargo ships carried the difference.** At least half of
   what arrived from Mar-Jul came by road or general cargo ship.
2. **Goods with another way in held up**: GCC goods by road, light goods probably by air.
3. **Imports had come back about two-thirds of the way by Jun-Jul**, with vehicles,
   clothing, East Asia and the Americas lagging; port figures suggest adapting continued after Hormuz closed again.

Still to do after step 7, as agreed: the "what if" range for the road's own share, and whether products that relied on
only a few supplier countries were hit harder.
